title: Greenfield control plane init operator checklist
content:
Purpose
This is an operator-focused checklist and run-through for initializing a greenfield private control plane (VPC or on-prem) using our Terraform modules and the private-controlplane-operator. It is written for the first operator on-call during a customer cutover or internal POC. The goal is to give a repeatable, auditable sequence: preflight, bootstrap, validation, scale, upgrade/rotation, and rollback paths.

Context and assumptions
- Target: private control plane components (control-plane API, console, controlplane-operator, KMS integration, audit logging).
- Infrastructure: either customer VPC (AWS/GCP) or on-prem baremetal using our terraform modules (module names: cp-network, cp-compute, cp-storage, cp-operator).
- Kubernetes: control-plane runs on a managed k8s distribution (EKS/GKE/PKS) or a customer-provided cluster; operator deploys CRDs for model-routing/state.
- Secrets: KMS/HSM integration expected for production; initial POC may use encrypted SSM/SecretsManager.
- Timebox: greenfield bootstrap ~4–6 hours for VPC with infra already approved; on-prem is variable.

Preflight (must complete before terraform apply)
- Confirm sign-offs and access:
  - Slack channel for the cutover created (e.g., #cp-greenfield-aisha).
  - Customer IT contact and platform SRE on standby.
  - Verify API keys, org IDs, and billing contacts.
- Verify Terraform state backend access:
  - Confirm remote state bucket/secret (s3/gcs/consul) is accessible and locked.
  - If using local state for POC, ensure encryption and a post-run manual check-in step.
- Validate variables and secrets:
  - tfvars checked into secure location; run tfvars lint script.
  - KMS key ARN (or HSM slot id) allocated and accessible from bootstrap host.
- Network and DNS:
  - VPC CIDR, public/private subnets, NAT/IGW, and cross-account peering details finalized.
  - DNS zone ownership confirmed and delegation records staged but not pointed.
- Ports and firewall:
  - Control-plane nodes need inbound ports: 6443 (k8s API), 443 (tls), 9090 (metrics), and operator-specific ports; confirm Firewall policies.
- Capacity planning:
  - Initial node pool sizes from cp-compute module: describe instance types, disk sizes, and expected cpu/memory headroom for 30% peak.
  - PV storage class IRL (storage class parameters for on-prem LVM/NAS) validated.
- Backups and snapshots:
  - Stateful components (postgres, etcd if applicable) snapshot schedule defined.
  - Vault/KMS key backup procedure documented.

Bootstrap sequence (step-by-step)
1) Preparation (local machine or bastion)
   - Export credentials: AWS/GCP creds, kubectl context, and terraform workspace.
   - Confirm terraform version matches module constraints (run `tfenv use` if necessary).
   - Pull latest modules: `git clone` and `git submodule update --init --recursive` for tf modules.
2) Dry-run (plan only)
   - `terraform init -backend-config=...`
   - `terraform plan -var-file=greenfield.tfvars -out plan.tfplan`
   - Share plan artifact with reviewers; wait for +1.
3) Apply infra modules in order (apply each module logically):
   - cp-network -> cp-storage -> cp-compute -> cp-operator-bindings
   - Apply cp-network first to create VPC/subnets and networking resources.
   - After network apply, run basic connectivity tests (ping, traceroute to bastion IPs).
4) Bootstrapping k8s control plane
   - Create node pools with labels expected by operator (e.g., `node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane=true`).
   - Install CNI and validate pod networking between nodes.
   - Deploy operator namespace and CRDs (apply CRDs only, no controllers yet if you want staged rollout).
5) Operator install and CR reconciliation
   - Deploy operator controller with `imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent` for initial stability.
   - Apply minimal CR that creates control-plane services (e.g., api endpoints, console).
   - Watch reconcile logs: `kubectl -n redwood-operator logs -l app=private-operator -f`
6) Secrets and KMS integration
   - Create KMS alias and attach IAM roles to node pool/service account.
   - Rotate minimal secret into Vault/SecretsManager and validate operator can read it via the bound role/service-account.
7) Smoke validation
   - API responds to health checks (HTTP 200 /healthz).
   - Console login works with SSO/OIDC test account.
   - Operator metrics present in the prometheus endpoint; basic alerts fire into the Slack channel.

Validation checklist (post-bootstrap)
- End-to-end control-plane request: submit test inference request using a small test model; verify response latency and correctness.
- Token-level billing hook: send synthetic traffic and verify cost metrics appear in console.
- Audit logs: confirm audit events propagate to logging backend and are queryable.
- Autoscaling smoke: scale up a simulated job and observe pod/node scale behavior and queuing/backpressure.
- Failover: cordon + drain one control-plane node, ensure no sustained errors and that operator reconciles.

Scaling guidance
- Horizontal scaling (node pools): scale by workload class (cpu-bound vs. io-bound). Use cp-compute module var `node_pool_profiles` to define profiles.
- Vertical scaling (instance types): use when hot-path latency demands change but validate with perf harness.
- Autoscaling buffer: set target utilization at 60–70% to handle bursts.
- Batching: enable operator-level batching for serving components to reduce token cost; validate latency percentiles.

Upgrade & key rotation plan (operator + infra upgrades)
- Upgrade policy and windowing:
  - Always perform upgrades in a canary namespace/pool first (10% of capacity, isolated traffic).
  - Use rollout: `canary -> gradual -> full` with automated health gates.
- Terraform module upgrades:
  - Treat module version bumps as changes to the infra plan. Run `terraform plan` and validate drift.
  - For breaking changes, create a migration tfvars and run in a staging workspace.
- Operator image upgrades:
  - Publish canary image tag, deploy to canary node pool and run smoke tests for 60–90 minutes.
  - If stable, incrementally roll to remaining pools with a max disruption of 1 pool at a time.
- KMS rotation:
  - Create a new key alias and grant operator access; perform in-memory double-read: operator should be able to read both current and new key for a transitional window.
  - Re-encrypt long-lived secrets in a maintenance window and update secret references.
  - Test rollback by re-pointing alias to previous key (validate decrypt).

Common failure modes and recovery steps
- Terraform state lock failure:
  - If lock persists, confirm owner via state backend UI; if owner process crashed, follow documented force-unlock procedure and audit logs.
- Operator stuck reconciling due to image pull errors:
  - Check node egress/NAT, image repository auth, and imagePullSecrets.
- KMS access denied after node reprovision:
  - Verify IAM role binding to node instance profile/service account; check STS token expiration and kubelet identity.
- Database migration partial failure:
  - Do NOT run a second migration. Revert to snapshot, run migration in a maintenance window, and notify customers.

Rollback checklist (if apply fails)
- If terraform apply introduces regression and cannot be fixed quickly:
  - Run `terraform state` to inspect changed resources and manually revert critical resources to previous values where possible.
  - Restore from snapshots for stateful components (postgres/etcd).
  - Re-point DNS records to previous endpoints immediately.
  - Escalation: page eng-private-sre, on-call DB and security leads.

Post-mortem and handoff
- Immediately capture a run log (commands executed, plan artifacts, and tfstate diffs) and upload to the cutover ticket.
- Fill out the cutover checklist template: all preflight items, approvals, plan timestamps, mitigation steps taken.
- Schedule a 30–60 minute sync with customer and platform SRE within 24 hours to review metrics and outstanding action items.

Operator notes / Terraform module pitfalls (lessons learned)
- Avoid in-place renames of module outputs that are used by other stacks — prefer new outputs + staged migration.
- Ensure module variables have defaults that are safe for POC; e.g., `enable_persistent_storage = false` by default for test clusters.
- Break large modules into smaller ones to reduce blast radius on apply.
- Keep a small helper script `validate-kms-access.sh` that runs from a bastion and simulates operator key reads.

Quick commands cheat sheet
- Terraform plan: `terraform plan -var-file=greenfield.tfvars -out plan.tfplan`
- Terraform apply: `terraform apply plan.tfplan`
- Force unlock: `terraform force-unlock <LOCK-ID>` (use cautiously)
- Watch operator logs: `kubectl -n redwood-operator logs -l app=private-operator -f`
- Reconcile CR: `kubectl -n redwood-operator delete pod -l app=private-operator` to force restart
- Test KMS read from pod: `kubectl exec -n redwood-operator -it <pod> -- /bin/sh -c "/bin/check-kms.sh"`

Appendix: validation checklist (copyable)
- [ ] Slack channel created and pinned docs attached
- [ ] Terraform plan artifact uploaded and reviewed
- [ ] Network and DNS preflight complete
- [ ] KMS key prepared and IAM roles assigned
- [ ] Operator CRDs installed and validated
- [ ] Minimal CR created and reconciled successfully
- [ ] E2E inference test passed (latency, correctness)
- [ ] Autoscaling and failover smoke tests passed
- [ ] Backup snapshots scheduled and verified
- [ ] Post-cutover sync scheduled

Notes to self
- Keep the greenfield sequence short and repeatable; very long one-off procedures lead to drift and undocumented exceptions.
- Consider a lightweight playbook runner to store plan artifacts and attach logs automatically to the cutover ticket next time.

-- Aisha R.
